html:
The arrival of the 1918 flu pandemic in Western Samoa, which killed about a fifth of its people in a few weeks of late 1918. It was among the worst death rates anywhere in the world.

New Zealand had seized German Samoa at the start of the First World War and governed it. In November 1918 the ship Talune came from Auckland carrying sick passengers. The administrator let it land with no quarantine. Influenza spread through every village, killing many adults and leaving few people well enough to bury the dead or gather food.

Next door, the governor of American Samoa closed his islands to ships, and there were no flu deaths there. The New Zealand administrator turned down help from the Americans.

Samoans did not forget. The disaster fed the Mau movement, which campaigned against New Zealand rule in the 1920s and 1930s. Samoa became independent in 1962, and in 2002 New Zealand's prime minister formally apologised for the epidemic and other wrongs. A similar story played out in Fiji with the measles epidemic of 1875.
